The blood consists of many important cell types. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) contain round nuclei and include lymphocytes - T cells, B cells, and natural killer (NK) cells - and monocytes. Cells that have multi-lobed nuclei include neutrophils, basophils, and eosinophils. Cells without nuclei include erythrocytes and platelets. These cell types are typically defined by the marker proteins expressed on their surface, but this definition can be qualitative and arbitrary. Furthermore, although the basics of hematopoiesis - or how blood cells develop (see diagram below) - are well-understood, the true relationship between cell types is highly complex and difficult to disentangle.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "600px"}
knitr::include_graphics("Hematopoiesis_simple.png")
```

(By A. Rad and M. Häggström. CC-BY-SA 3.0 license)

By capturing information across the full genome, single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) allows us to build a more comprehensive and unbiased view of cell types and their relationships to each other. Download the data file `PBMC_scaled_variable.txt` from the D2L site, under Content->Datasets->PBMC. This dataset consists of single-cell gene expression profiles of 2,638 PBMCs extracted from normal blood. The data have been preprocessed by centering, scaling, log-transforming, and choosing the most informative genes. 

```{r echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library("patchwork")
library("tidyverse")
pbmc.data <- read.table("PBMC_scaled_variable.txt")
```

(Note how difficult it is to define discrete cell types using single marker genes that are expressed on a continuum.)

***Color the PCA plot by each marker genes (6 plots total).***

```{r}
# Define function to create plot
plot_pcaexp <- function(pca, data, marker_gene, cell_type){
  #combine first two PCAs and expression into one df
  plotting_data <- cbind(as.data.frame(pca$x[, c("PC1", "PC2")]),
                         expression = data[, marker_gene])
  #create plot
  ggplot(plotting_data, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, col = expression)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
    scale_color_gradient(low="dark blue",high="cyan") +
    labs(col = cell_type)
}
```

```{r}
#make plots
bcell <- plot_pcaexp(cells_pca, pbmc.data, "MS4A1", "B-cell")
monos <- plot_pcaexp(cells_pca, pbmc.data, "LYZ", "Monocyte")
plates <- plot_pcaexp(cells_pca, pbmc.data, "PPBP", "Platelet")
tcell <- plot_pcaexp(cells_pca, pbmc.data, "IL7R", "T-cell")
nkcell <- plot_pcaexp(cells_pca, pbmc.data, "GNLY", "NK cell")
dendros <- plot_pcaexp(cells_pca, pbmc.data, "FCER1A", "Dendritic cell")
```

```{r}
#display plots
wrap_plots(bcell, nkcell, tcell, monos, plates, dendros, ncol = 3)
```

### Problem 3

Let's perform hierarchical clustering on the first 200 cells (i.e., rows of the original dataset).

```{r}
pbmc.subset <- pbmc.data[1:200,]
```

Here is a new version of the plotColoredTree function that is specifically configured for the PBMC data format. 

```{r echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(ggdendro)

plotColoredTree.PBMC <- function(hc, label_vector, color_vector){
  # Convert clusters object into a dataframe
  hcdata<- dendro_data(hc, type="rectangle")
  # Add additional columns used for plotting to that dataframe
  labeldf <- data.frame(index=1:length(label_vector),newlabel=label_vector,color=color_vector,name=names(label_vector))
  hcdata$labels <- merge(x=hcdata$labels, y=labeldf,  by.x="label", by.y="name")
  temp <- ggplot() +
    # Plot the tree
    geom_segment(data=segment(hcdata), aes(x=x, y=y, xend=xend, yend=yend)) +
    # Label the tips
    geom_text(data=label(hcdata), aes(x=x, y=y, label=newlabel, colour = color, hjust=0), size=3) + 
    # Additonal formatting instructions
    coord_flip() + theme_dendro() +  scale_y_reverse(expand=c(0.2, 0))
  print(temp)
}
```

### Problem 6

To better understand the neurobiological basis of heroin addiction, the Hurd Lab used microarrays to measure gene expression in the nucleus accumbens of deceased heroin users and control individuals. The nucleus accumbens is a brain region that plays a central role in the regulation of reward, emotion, motivation and goal-directed behavior. 

#### Problem 6.a

Our first step is to get the data. First, go to the [appropriate GEO entry](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE87823).
Conveniently, GEO provides a nice service to preprocess the data. To access it, click on the link for ``Analyze with GEO2R''.

To run the analysis, you'll first need to define two groups to assign samples to.
To do so, click on the little link for "Define Groups", which will drop down a small menu.
To create the group "heroin", type "heroin" into the text box and hit enter.
Then do the same for the group "control".
(Note: For this homework it is important that you create the groups in this order, so that logFC > 0 means upregulated in heroin user samples.)
To assign samples to the heroin group, select the corresponding 22 samples then click the "heroin" location in the "Define groups" drop down.
(Note: You can shift-click on the sample list to select multiple samples at once.)
Next, assign the remaining 27 samples to the control group.
Lastly, scroll down on the page and click the "Analyze" button.

Once the analysis results appear, you'll see a sorted list of genes with their expression difference between heroin vs control.

**Can you interpret any biology of heroin addiction from the top differentially expressed genes?**

*Answer:*

#### Problem 6.d

To make sense of these data, we'll look for enrichment in gene sets defined by the [Human Phenotype Ontology](https://hpo.jax.org/). I downloaded the gene sets from the [Molecular Signatures Database](https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb/) and processed them into an R list of character vectors for easy loading. You can download the processed gene sets from d2l -> Content -> Datasets -> HurdHeroinGeneExpression.
```{r eval=F}
db <- readRDS('c5.hpo.v7.4.symbols.rds')
```

We'll define a function to calculate the p-value for Fisher's Exact Test to test for enrichment of a gene set in the upregulated genes. (Note that you may need to change some variable names from our previous function.) In the code below `gs` will be the name of the gene set we're testing.

```{r eval=F}
enrichment_pval <- function(gs) {
  ul <- tib %>% filter((Gene.symbol %in% db[[gs]]) & upregulated) %>% nrow()
  ur <- tib %>% filter((Gene.symbol %in% db[[gs]]) & !upregulated) %>% nrow()
  ll <- tib %>% filter(!(Gene.symbol %in% db[[gs]]) & upregulated) %>% nrow()
  lr <- tib %>% filter(!(Gene.symbol %in% db[[gs]]) & !upregulated) %>% nrow()
  table <- matrix(c(ul,ll,ur,lr), nrow=2)
  # The return value from our function is the result of the last line in it
  fisher.test(table,alternative="greater")$p.value
}
```

Then we can use `map_dbl` to apply this function to all gene sets. (This may take a couple of minutes.)

```{r eval=F, cache=TRUE}
all_pvals <- map_dbl(names(db), enrichment_pval)
all_tests <- tibble(set=names(db), p.value=all_pvals)
all_tests <- all_tests %>% arrange(p.value)
```

**Which gene set has the most significant p-value?**

*Answer:*

#### Problem 6.e

Here we add a column to your tibble that contains Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values.
```{r eval=F}
m <- nrow(all_tests)
all_tests <- all_tests %>% mutate(fdr=p.value*m/1:m)
```
